passages.where: Jacob loves Joseph more than his other sons and gives him a robe to show it, and the brothers hate Joseph and cannot speak a kind word to him. The site's plain note says the brothers' pain was real even though what they did with it was evil, and that Jacob's sin was to show his favor and build a home around it. The note on chapter 45 observes that this family's estrangement begins with speech that cannot happen, and ends years later when the brothers can talk with Joseph again.

The psalmist has become a stranger to his brothers and a foreigner to his own mother's sons, and he says it is because zeal for God's house has consumed him. The site's note describes him as estranged from his brothers and mocked for his devotion. Some estrangements come from faithfulness rather than from sin, and the Bible gives the one who carries that loss a prayer.

Twenty years after he deceived his brother and fled, Jacob hears that Esau is coming toward him with four hundred men, and he is terrified. The note says the center of his prayer is a confession that he is too small for the faithful love God has shown him, followed by a plain request for rescue from his brother. Going back toward someone you wronged, or someone who wronged you, can be frightening, and Jacob takes the fear to God before he takes a step.

Isaac dies old and full of years, and Esau and Jacob bury him together. The site's note says the brothers' last scene together is a graveside, and that the rivalry which began in the womb ends in a shared duty. The plain note asks whether there is someone you are estranged from whom you will one day stand beside, at a grave or before God, and whether peace has to wait that long.

When their herdsmen quarrel, Abram asks Lot that there be no contention between them, because they are brothers, and offers him the first choice of the land. The note says Abram appeals to kinship rather than to his rank and lets the younger man decide. Sometimes the way to keep peace in a family is to live apart without hostility, and Abram shows that a separation can be generous.

David allows his banished son Absalom to come home but will not see his face, and two years pass before the king receives him with a kiss. The site's note says the problem was not that David wanted his son back, but that neither justice nor real repentance was part of the return, and the half-made peace led straight to revolt. A reunion that skips the truth rarely holds.

Paul and Barnabas disagree so sharply over taking Mark, who had deserted them on their earlier mission, that they part company and go different ways. Luke records the break without hiding it, and both men go on serving. Years later, writing from prison, Paul asks Timothy to bring Mark with him because he is useful in the ministry (2 Timothy 4:11).

When the younger son comes home, his father sees him far off, is filled with compassion and runs to him before he can finish his speech. The site's note calls this the emotional center of the chapter, and the parable shows what God is like toward anyone who turns home. The plain note adds a word for anyone whose own father was absent or hurt them: the story does not ask them to pretend otherwise, and it tells them they have a Father in heaven who is not like that.

The older son is angry and refuses to go in, and his father comes out to plead with him too; the story ends without saying whether he goes in. The site's plain note speaks to parents of a child they cannot reach: the story does not promise that every child will come home, or say when, but it shows a Father who watches the road and goes out to plead. It counsels keeping the door open as far as you safely can, and praying.

Paul tells believers to live at peace with everyone, and he adds two conditions: if it is possible, and on your part. The site's plain note on the chapter says that blessing an enemy and refusing revenge never means staying in danger or keeping silent about harm. You answer for your part of the peace, not for the other person's.

The Old Testament closes with God's promise to send Elijah before the great day of the LORD, to turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the hearts of children to their fathers. In Luke the angel tells Zechariah that his son John will go in the spirit and power of Elijah to do this work (Luke 1:17). The healing of broken families is something God has promised to do, not only a task he has left to us.

misread.taken: Jesus' saying that a disciple must hate father and mother is sometimes taken as permission to cut family off without grief, and some groups have used it to separate people from their parents, husbands, wives or children, or to make estrangement a sign of special devotion.
misread.says: The site's plain note on the chapter says Jesus asks for first place, not for cruelty. The same Jesus repeated the command to honor father and mother, made sure his own mother was cared for from the cross, and the New Testament says that one who will not provide for his own household has denied the faith. The note says plainly that groups which have used this verse to cut people off from their families have read it wrongly, and that the division Jesus speaks of comes from others' response to him, not from his followers' hostility. It also speaks to believers whose families have rejected them for their faith: they are not alone, they have not failed, and if rejection has turned into threats or harm, seeking safety is not disloyalty to Jesus.

whole: If you stepped away from a family member because they were hurting you or your children, or if anyone in your family is threatening you now, your safety comes first. Tell someone you trust and get help; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn, and no verse in the Bible asks you to go back into danger. Estrangement is a grief with no funeral. A parent keeps a phone that does not ring and a chair that no one sits in. An adult child blocks a number and then lies awake wondering whether it was cruel. A brother learns from a cousin that his sister has had a baby. Some estrangements follow one terrible day; many follow years of small injuries that no one would name. Often the two sides tell different stories, each true to what it lived: the parent may honestly not know why, and the child may have tried to say why many times without being heard. Christians often carry an added weight, the sense that a family which loves God should never end up here, and that someone must be the villain.

Scripture does not tell this story only one way. Jacob favored Joseph, and the brothers could not speak a kind word to him. Jacob deceived Esau and spent twenty years afraid of him. David let Absalom come home but would not see his face, a return without truth or repentance that ended in revolt. Paul and Barnabas parted company over Mark. And the psalmist became a stranger to his brothers because of his zeal for God. Behind the breaks the Bible records are favoritism, deceit, harm left unnamed, silence, pride, and sometimes faithfulness itself. None of this means the blame is always shared, or shared equally: sometimes one person did real harm and the other is right to keep away. It means only that families in Scripture fracture the way ours do, and that most of us find it easier to tell our own estrangement with ourselves as the one wronged. That may be true. It is seldom the whole of the truth for anyone.

So the Bible's wisdom holds both people in view, and it does not tell either of them that everything is their fault. For the one who stepped away, distance from someone who harms you is not the sin that Jesus' hard saying about father and mother is sometimes made to condemn, and it is not a failure to honor. Live at peace if it is possible, on your part; sometimes the honest peace is a boundary, kept without hatred, as Abram and Lot parted without contention. No one is required to go back to danger, and no one may use Scripture to make them. For the parent or brother or sister who has been left, the father in Luke watches the road and runs when the son turns, but he does not drag him home, and he goes out to plead with the son who will not come in while leaving him free. Ask what the other person has been trying to say, and listen without defending. Offer an apology for what you can see you did, without conditions and without a lecture attached. Respect a request for space, and do not recruit relatives or the church to apply pressure. A pastor or a counselor who understands family breakdown can help either side, and both can pray.

The hope Scripture gives begins with God, not with us. In Christ God reconciled the world to himself, at his own cost, and that is the pattern for every true reconciliation: it is costly, it tells the truth, and it is never forced. The Old Testament ends with God's promise to turn the hearts of fathers and children toward one another. Esau and Jacob stood together at their father's grave; years after the sharpest quarrel in Acts, Paul asked for Mark. Not every estrangement is mended in this life, and the Bible does not promise that yours will be. But God settles the lonely in families, he has not stopped loving the one who left or the one who was left, and in the resurrection he has promised that what is broken will not have the last word.
sit: If you are the one who stepped away, what would a safe and honest door look like from your side; and if you are the one who was left, what has the other person been trying to tell you that you have not yet been able to hear?

prayer.lead: A prayer for a lonely and troubled heart that also asks God to take away its own sins. Both sides of an estrangement can pray it honestly.

careLines.text: Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger.
If rejection has turned into threats or harm, seeking safety is not disloyalty to Jesus.
If your own father was absent, or hurt you, this story is not asking you to pretend otherwise.
Keep the door open as far as you safely can, and keep praying.
God has not stopped loving your child, and he has not stopped loving you.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
